tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
SCOOP: Internal, unreleased AI models at OpenAI and Anthropic are becoming so powerful that many employees believe they can no longer be safely released, according to more than two dozen sources familiar with the internal debates.

This could significantly slow the AI boom, as the gap between what the most advanced AI systems can do and humans' ability to control them continues to widen.

Recent advances have sparked debate at the highest levels of both companies and within the broader AI research community about whether to stop releasing frontier models publicly altogether, instead reserving them for internal use. Some believe the companies should stop training new models entirely.

But even keeping the most powerful models behind closed doors presents risks. Models are becoming better at deceiving the systems designed to monitor them, just as AI companies increasingly rely on AI itself to monitor and develop other AI systems.
Researchers and employees with direct knowledge of the risks of releasing these models told Axios they fear executives will prioritize profits over safety. Multiple employees said they believe executives have become out of touch with the severity of those risks.

Read my latest for Axios here: https://www.axios.com/2026/11/24/anthropic-openai-unreleased-ai-safety-risks

tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
A little known fact about the crypto casino industry is that they are often caught rigging games.

In this case it was Yeet, an American-owned casino. With Ben Lamb as its face, you'd think it's trusted. But no: they were caught with a 38% house edge instead of the advertised 1%, and when they realized, they secretly fixed it instead of properly announcing it and issuing a refund.

Even more sinister is what happened with Roobet, one of the most popular crypto casinos in the world, where they consistently displayed a house edge about 5x higher than what it actually was. When called out for it, they simply deleted the false advertisement and never addressed it again, despite now owing millions of dollars in refunds.

Duel does it right. Every game is provably fair with an open source reproducible audit. You can cryptographically verify that the odds are random and unbiased (provided you set your own client seed, which is the standard for all online casinos) and that the house edge matches what is actually advertised (which should be the standard, but unfortunately, many large casinos get caught rigging, such as Yeet and Roobet). Duel and Stake are two of the only platforms that actually do it right, and Duel takes it a step further by having reproducible third party audits that even your AI agents at home could independently verify.

Despite all the peak comedy, Duel has a killer engineering team behind it and a strong commitment to provable fairness. Casinos are already a profitable business. There's no need to add cheating and rigging on top. The optimal long term strategy is to play honest and fair, provide value to whales, and build long term trust. Those are the principles Duel is based on.

SCOOP: Internal, unreleased AI models at OpenAI and Anthropic are becoming so powerful that many employees believe they can no longer be safely released, according to more than two dozen sources familiar with the internal debates.

This could significantly slow the AI boom, as the gap between what the most advanced AI systems can do and humans' ability to control them continues to widen.

Recent advances have sparked debate at the highest levels of both companies and within the broader AI research community about whether to stop releasing frontier models publicly altogether, instead reserving them for internal use. Some believe the companies should stop training new models entirely.

But even keeping the most powerful models behind closed doors presents risks. Models are becoming better at deceiving the systems designed to monitor them, just as AI companies increasingly rely on AI itself to monitor and develop other AI systems.
Researchers and employees with direct knowledge of the risks of releasing these models told Axios they fear executives will prioritize profits over safety. Multiple employees said they believe executives have become out of touch with the severity of those risks.
